## Goals

- Explain why a network that can fit random labels makes uniform
  generalization bounds based on the hypothesis class vacuous.
- Describe double descent: the test error as a function of model size,
  beyond the interpolation threshold.
- Derive the minimum-norm solution of an under-determined least-squares
  problem, and show that gradient descent from zero finds it.
- Reproduce both phenomena with small experiments (example notebooks 03
  and 05).

## Theory

### Classical expectations

The classical picture of model selection is a U-shaped test error: a small
model underfits (high bias), a large one overfits (high variance), and the
best model lies in between. Uniform convergence makes this quantitative.
For a class $\mathcal F$ of functions with values in $[-1, 1]$ and a sample
$S$ of size $n$, the empirical Rademacher complexity

$$
\hat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal F) = \E_\sigma \Bigl[ \sup_{f \in \mathcal F}
\frac1n \sum_{i=1}^n \sigma_i f(x_i) \Bigr],
\qquad \sigma_i \in \{-1, +1\} \text{ uniform},
$$ {#eq-rademacher}

measures how well $\mathcal F$ can correlate with random signs, and with
high probability the gap between the risk and the empirical risk of every
$f \in \mathcal F$ is at most of order
$\hat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal F) + \sqrt{\log(1/\delta)/n}$ (lecture 2).

### Fitting random labels

@zhang2017understanding trained standard image classifiers on data whose
labels had been replaced by random ones. The networks reached zero training
error, with test error at chance, using the same architecture,
optimizer and hyper-parameters that generalize well on the true labels.
Fitting random signs exactly means that the supremum in @eq-rademacher is
1 for (almost) every $\sigma$, so $\hat{\mathfrak R}_S = 1$, and the bound
says nothing: the capacity of the class reachable by training does not
explain why the same networks generalize on real labels. Explicit
regularization (weight decay, dropout) changed this only little; the
explanation must involve the data and the training algorithm, not only the
class.

### Double descent

@belkin2019reconciling observed that the U-curve is only the first part of
the story. As the number of parameters $p$ grows beyond the number of
samples $n$, the model can *interpolate* the training data, the training
error is zero, and the test error, after a peak at the *interpolation
threshold* $p \approx n$, decreases again, often to below the best
under-parametrized value. @nakkiran2020deep found the same shape in deep
networks as a function of width, of the number of training epochs, and of
the number of samples (more data can hurt near the threshold).

The simplest model that shows it is regression on random features
[@rahimi2007random]: a fixed random map
$\phi(x) = \operatorname{relu}(W x + b) \in \R^p$ and a linear readout
$\theta$ fitted by least squares on the feature matrix
$\Phi \in \R^{n \times p}$. For $p < n$ the least-squares solution is
unique. For $p \ge n$ there are infinitely many interpolating solutions,
and the natural choice is the one with the smallest norm,

$$
\theta^\dagger = \Phi^{+} y
= \Phi^\top (\Phi \Phi^\top)^{-1} y \quad (p \ge n,\ \operatorname{rank}\Phi = n),
\qquad
\lVert \theta^\dagger \rVert^2 = \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{(u_k^\top y)^2}{s_k^2},
$$ {#eq-min-norm}

where $\Phi = \sum_k s_k u_k v_k^\top$ is the singular value decomposition
and $\Phi^+$ the pseudo-inverse. Near $p = n$ the smallest singular value
$s_n$ of a random $n \times p$ matrix is close to 0, so fitting the noise in
$y$ requires a huge $\lVert\theta^\dagger\rVert$, and the predictions on new
points are wild: this is the peak. For $p \gg n$, all singular values are
bounded away from 0, and the noise is spread over many directions of
feature space where it does little harm. @bartlett2020benign characterize
when minimum-norm interpolation is even consistent ("benign overfitting"):
the data must have many directions of small variance that absorb the noise.

### The implicit bias of gradient descent

Gradient descent on $\frac12 \lVert \Phi\theta - y \rVert^2$ from
$\theta_0 = 0$ finds $\theta^\dagger$ without being told to. Every gradient
$\Phi^\top(\Phi\theta - y)$ lies in the row space of $\Phi$, so all iterates
do too; the limit interpolates (for a small enough step), and the only
interpolating solution in the row space is $\theta^\dagger$
(Exercise 7.1). The training algorithm, not only the model class, decides
which interpolating solution we get. For deep networks the implicit bias
is not known in general, but this linear case is exact for the readout of
random features and, in the lazy regime of @sec-ntk, approximately for a
whole wide network.

## Where in the code

::: {.callout-note title="Where in the code"}
These phenomena need no new library code; they are experiments with what
earlier chapters built. The random features are an untrained
`{python} api_link("glassnn.nn.Linear")` followed by
`{python} api_link("glassnn.nn.ReLU")`, evaluated under
`{python} api_link("glassnn.no_grad")`; the minimum-norm readout is
`numpy.linalg.pinv`. The memorization experiments train an MLP with
`{python} api_link("glassnn.optim.AdamW")`, whose decoupled weight decay is
the shrinkage of @eq-weight-decay
(`{python} src_link("glassnn.optim.Adam.step")`).

The full experiments, with more seeds and more settings, are the example
notebooks
[`03_double_descent`](https://github.com/bioinfo-recetox/glassnn/blob/main/examples/03_double_descent.ipynb)
and
[`05_memorizing_noise`](https://github.com/bioinfo-recetox/glassnn/blob/main/examples/05_memorizing_noise.ipynb).
Their expected findings are asserted, at a smaller scale, by
`tests/test_examples.py`, so they are checked on every change of the
library.
:::

## Try it

### Double descent with random features

The setting of notebook 03: a sparse linear signal in 20 dimensions with
noise standard deviation 0.1, $n = 100$ training samples, and $p$ random
ReLU features.

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

import glassnn.functional as F
from glassnn import Tensor, backend, manual_seed, nn, no_grad, optim
from glassnn.data import DataLoader

backend.set_default_dtype("float64")


def sparse_regression(n, seed, d=20, k=5, noise=0.1):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    beta = np.zeros(d)
    beta[:k] = 1 / np.sqrt(k)
    X = rng.normal(size=(n, d))
    return X, X @ beta + noise * rng.normal(size=n)


N_TRAIN = 100
X_train, y_train = sparse_regression(N_TRAIN, seed=0)
X_test, y_test = sparse_regression(2000, seed=1)


def random_features(p, seed):
    manual_seed(seed)
    features = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(20, p), nn.ReLU())
    with no_grad():
        return features(Tensor(X_train)).data, features(Tensor(X_test)).data


def test_error(p, seed):
    phi_train, phi_test = random_features(p, seed)
    theta = np.linalg.pinv(phi_train) @ y_train
    return np.mean((phi_test @ theta - y_test) ** 2)


widths = np.unique(np.r_[np.geomspace(5, 3000, 25).round().astype(int), N_TRAIN])
errors = [np.median([test_error(p, seed) for seed in range(5)]) for p in widths]

plt.figure(figsize=(6, 3.5))
plt.loglog(widths, errors, "o-", markersize=3)
plt.axvline(N_TRAIN, color="gray", linestyle=":")
plt.xlabel("number of random features $p$")
plt.ylabel("test MSE (median of 5 seeds)")
plt.show()
```

The test error peaks at $p = n = 100$ and then falls to below its best
value for $p < n$.

### Gradient descent finds the minimum-norm solution

With $p = 300 > n$, gradient descent on the readout from $\theta = 0$, here
written with GlassNN tensors, converges to the pseudo-inverse solution:

```{python}
phi_train, _ = random_features(300, seed=0)
theta_dagger = np.linalg.pinv(phi_train) @ y_train

Phi, y = Tensor(phi_train), Tensor(y_train)
theta = Tensor(np.zeros(300), requires_grad=True)
step = 1.0 / np.linalg.norm(phi_train, 2) ** 2  # below 2 / largest eigenvalue
for _ in range(20000):
    theta.grad = None
    (0.5 * ((Phi @ theta - y) ** 2).sum()).backward()
    theta = Tensor(theta.data - step * theta.grad.data, requires_grad=True)

print("training residual:      ", np.abs(phi_train @ theta.data - y_train).max())
print("distance to pinv(Φ) y:  ", np.linalg.norm(theta.data - theta_dagger))
print("norms (GD, pinv):       ", np.linalg.norm(theta.data), np.linalg.norm(theta_dagger))
```

### Memorizing random labels

The setting of notebook 05: 200 Gaussian points in 20 dimensions, labels
given by a hyperplane, and an MLP with two hidden layers of width 256
(about 72 000 parameters), trained with AdamW.

```{python}
backend.set_default_dtype("float32")
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
w_star = rng.normal(size=20)


def sample(n):
    X = rng.normal(size=(n, 20))
    return X, (X @ w_star > 0).astype(np.int64)


X_tr, y_tr = sample(200)
X_te, y_te = sample(2000)
y_random = rng.integers(0, 2, size=200)


def accuracy(model, X, y):
    with no_grad():
        return float((model(Tensor(X)).data.argmax(axis=1) == y).mean())


def train(labels, epochs=40):
    manual_seed(0)
    model = nn.Sequential(
        nn.Linear(20, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 2)
    )
    optimizer = optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3, weight_decay=0.0)
    history = []
    for _ in range(epochs):
        for xb, yb in DataLoader(X_tr, labels, batch_size=32, shuffle=True):
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            F.cross_entropy(model(xb), yb).backward()
            optimizer.step()
        history.append((accuracy(model, X_tr, labels), accuracy(model, X_te, y_te)))
    return np.array(history)


fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))
for labels, name in [(y_tr, "true labels"), (y_random, "random labels")]:
    history = train(labels)
    ax.plot(history[:, 0], label=f"{name}: train")
    ax.plot(history[:, 1], "--", label=f"{name}: test")
ax.set_xlabel("epoch")
ax.set_ylabel("accuracy")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.show()
```

Both label sets are fitted perfectly, the random ones about three times
more slowly; on the random labels the test accuracy stays at chance.
Notebook 05 adds partially corrupted labels, weight decay and early
stopping: only a very strong weight decay prevents the memorization of
random labels, and with 30 % flipped labels the validation accuracy is best
before the training accuracy reaches 100 %.

## Exercises

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise 7.1: gradient descent from zero"}
Let $\Phi \in \R^{n\times p}$ with $p > n$ have rank $n$. (a) Show that
$\theta^\dagger = \Phi^\top(\Phi\Phi^\top)^{-1}y$ interpolates and has the
smallest norm among all interpolating $\theta$. (b) Show that gradient
descent on $\frac12\lVert\Phi\theta - y\rVert^2$ from $\theta_0 = 0$ with
step $\eta < 2/s_1^2$ converges to $\theta^\dagger$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}
(a) $\Phi\theta^\dagger = y$. Any interpolating $\theta$ is
$\theta^\dagger + v$ with $\Phi v = 0$; $\theta^\dagger = \Phi^\top a$ lies
in the row space, so $v \perp \theta^\dagger$ and
$\lVert\theta\rVert^2 = \lVert\theta^\dagger\rVert^2 + \lVert v\rVert^2$.
(b) Each update adds $-\eta\Phi^\top(\Phi\theta_t - y)$, a vector of the
row space, so $\theta_t = \Phi^\top a_t$ for all $t$. The residual
$r_t = \Phi\theta_t - y$ obeys $r_{t+1} = (I - \eta\Phi\Phi^\top) r_t$,
which tends to 0 when all eigenvalues $s_k^2$ of $\Phi\Phi^\top$ satisfy
$|1 - \eta s_k^2| < 1$. The limit interpolates and lies in the row space,
and $\theta^\dagger$ is the only such vector.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise 7.2: ridge against the peak"}
Replace the minimum-norm readout by ridge regression,
$\theta_\lambda = (\Phi^\top\Phi + \lambda I)^{-1}\Phi^\top y$, for
$\lambda \in \{10^{-3}, 10^{-1}, 1\}$, and plot the test error against $p$.
*Hint:* $\theta_\lambda = \Phi^\top(\Phi\Phi^\top + \lambda I)^{-1} y$
needs only an $n \times n$ solve.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}
```{python}
backend.set_default_dtype("float64")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))
for lam in [0.0, 1e-3, 1e-1, 1.0]:
    curve = []
    for p in widths:
        errors_p = []
        for seed in range(5):
            phi_train, phi_test = random_features(p, seed)
            if lam == 0.0:
                theta = np.linalg.pinv(phi_train) @ y_train
            else:  # the n x n form of the hint
                gram = phi_train @ phi_train.T + lam * np.eye(N_TRAIN)
                theta = phi_train.T @ np.linalg.solve(gram, y_train)
            errors_p.append(np.mean((phi_test @ theta - y_test) ** 2))
        curve.append(np.median(errors_p))
    ax.loglog(widths, curve, "o-", markersize=3, label=rf"$\lambda = {lam}$")
ax.axvline(N_TRAIN, color="gray", linestyle=":")
ax.set_xlabel("$p$")
ax.set_ylabel("test MSE")
ax.legend()
plt.show()
```

The penalty bounds $\lVert\theta\rVert$ and removes the peak; with
$\lambda = 1$ the test error decreases with $p$ throughout. A tiny
$\lambda$ only lowers the peak. The peak is a property of the
*unregularized* interpolating solution.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise 7.3: when more data hurts"}
Fix $p = 200$ and vary the number of training samples
$n \in \{50, 100, 150, 190, 200, 210, 300, 600\}$. Plot the test error of
the minimum-norm solution against $n$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}
The test error has a peak at $n = p = 200$: with 100 samples it is about
0.08, with 190 about 1, with 200 about 10, and it falls again for larger
$n$. Near the interpolation threshold, more data makes the model *worse*:
sample-wise double descent [@nakkiran2020deep].
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise 7.4: Rademacher complexity of the trained network"}
Use the random-label experiment to estimate the empirical Rademacher
complexity of "the functions this training procedure can reach": draw a
few sign vectors $\sigma$, train on them, and compute
$\frac1n\sum_i\sigma_i f(x_i)$ with $f = $ the sign of the predicted class
score. What value do you get, and what does it mean for the bound?
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}
The network fits every $\sigma$ perfectly, so each term is 1 and the
estimate is 1, the largest possible value. A bound of the form
"risk $\le$ empirical risk $+ 2\hat{\mathfrak R}_S + \dots$" is then larger
than 1 and says nothing about the classifier trained on the true labels,
although its test accuracy is about 0.89.
:::
